speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) what is the currently projected share or range of operating costs for the Thomson-East Coast MRT Line that is expected to be covered by fare revenues versus by Government grants and subsidies; and (b) in light of the financial difficulties faced by operators of the existing MRT Lines, what share or range of operating costs for these lines are expected to be covered by existing operators versus by Government grants and subsidies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: First, the Government fully bears the upfront cost of building new rail lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The major railway lines that are being constructed during this period are the Thomson-East Coast Line (TEL), Jurong Region Line and the Cross Island Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: When completed, there will be a total of eight MRT lines, and eight in 10 households will live within a 10-minute walk from a train station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Under the current financing model, the operating and maintenance costs (O&M) are fully borne by the rail operators, Singapore MRT (SMRT) Trains and Singapore Bus Services Transit (SBST).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The rail operators have intensified their O&M regimes over the past few years in order to raise reliability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Coupled with the Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) asset renewal, rail MRT reliability has improved considerably.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Last year, the MRT network achieved a Mean Kilometres Between Failure (MKBF) of 690,000 train-kilometres (km).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is a significant improvement of over three times from 2017, when the network MKBF was at 181,000 train-km.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These efforts at raising rail reliability are costly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They have taken a financial toll on the rail operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, roughly, the losses were about 10% of the operator's cost, and commuters' fare make up about 73% of the operator's cost.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, here, you see a new line – Downtown Line (DTL).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The loss was about 36% of operator's cost and commuter's fare income just made up about 52% of the operator's cost.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are combing through the results, but I believe Downtown Line continues to be in pretty bad shape.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In the case of TEL, the Government recognises that the ridership in the initial years will be uncertain as the line will be opening in multiple stages over six years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is a very long line, and, by necessity, we will be opening it stage by stage and you can imagine the long lead time taken to build up traffic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is unlike the arrangement for all the other railway lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will continue to work towards improving rail reliability, making our rail network among the most reliable in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Achieving such a goal requires a regular investment in substantial expenditures to support intensive maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will strike the right balance between what should be borne by taxpayers through direct Government funding, by commuters through fares, and by operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are, however, mindful that any decision to increase the level of Government funding for rail operations has to be weighed against competing needs, such as healthcare and security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have one clarification and two supplementary questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Government bears the revenue risk and is expected to subsidise the Line, at least in the initial years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For the supplementary questions, first: the fare set by the Public Transport Council (PTC), the formula which is valid until 2022, allows adjustments for capacity through the network capacity factor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the fare formula does not account for the increased tempo of maintenance expenditures which are going to be the responsibility of the legacy operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I would like to know what are the plans in the near term, for the current term of the current fare formula, what are the plans that the Ministry has if the operators continue to sustain substantial operating losses, which might threaten their commercial viability or affect their ability to carry out required maintenance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second supplementary question is: will the contracting model for the TEL be evaluated as an alternative to the new rail financing framework for the legacy lines and, if so, what would be the criteria for such an evaluation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before I end, I just would like to hope that Singaporeans appreciate the tremendous financial investments the Government is making to ensure that our rail system is safe and reliable.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: These are serious comments and obviously he has put a lot of thought and some research into this subject.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I have spent now more than three years in this difficult portfolio.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I have exercised a lot of my time and energy on this one.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Fortunately, after three years of hard work, we are beginning to see some results.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But do not forget, we are not yet out of the woods because, as I repeated in this House three years ago when I took on this job, the problem can be fixed, but it is a multi-year project.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It will take several years and multi billion dollars because you have to spend a lot of money.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is multi-year because the North-South, East-West Lines are old lines, and significant assets have to be renewed and replaced; and until they are completely renewed and replaced, well, you know, old trains are like old bodies.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: At 67, my flu hit me hard in the last couple of months.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When I was younger, three weeks, I am well, without any medication.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: This time took me more than two months.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: After the virus is cleared, it led to secondary cough, which I am still suffering.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is the worst thing because coughing is uncontrollable and it usually happens at night and, therefore, I do not get a good sleep.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And, as you know, to get well, you need sleep.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Sorry, for sharing with you my personal experience.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But looking after the train is the same as looking after the body.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: If you neglect your train, you will suffer for it.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When the trains are new, it does not matter because you do not experience the ill results of the negligence.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But for old trains, it will show up.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Do not forget, over the next 10-year period, it is not just Thomson Line, there is Jurong Region line and there is Cross Island line.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Again, those are long lines and, therefore, we will have no choice but to adopt the Financing Model based on a Gross Cost Model; otherwise, no operators will take on this tender.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But we have to be fair to operators and the other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is why we need wise men and women in the PTC.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Their job is to try to be fair and reasonable to operators as well as commuters.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Having pumped in the money, the second order question is: how do you share the burden?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And, really, you are talking about sharing between taxpayers through Government subsidy, or commuters through some fare adjustments.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I look to the PTC to think through this problem.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I am also spending some time thinking about it.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Now that I have a little bit more time to breathe, I will be focusing on this particular problem on the optimal model of financing MRT as well as buses.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is not clear whether a Gross Cost Model is superior to a Net Cost Model.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is also not clear whether buses should follow some model whereas MRT follows the other.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: My preliminary thinking is that it depends on the state of maturity of a particular bus package, or a particular MRT line.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When the line has reached steady state, with a predictable volume of commuter traffic, and if the market is competitive, then I think a Net Cost Model is suitable.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But when it is still in transition, and especially if the market is not naturally competitive, then I think a Gross Cost Model may be more relevant.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Again, because buses and rails are different, buses, if you call an international tender, there will be many bids.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: An MRT line actually is a local monopoly.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Inevitably, the Government has to come in to regulate the operator, and to make sure that there is no profiteering but, at the same time, be reasonable to the operator, because nobody will set up a company to bleed every year; they are not charities.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Our job is to make sure that they do not "gold-plate" the engineering department, in other words, overstate specifications, overdo things, pushing up costs and that they do not profiteer.
